```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE, warning = FALSE, message = FALSE,
                      fig.width = 8, fig.height = 5, dpi = 150)
```

```{r libraries}
library(tidyverse)
library(brms)
library(tidybayes)
library(ggrepel)
source("load_llm_data.R")
source("load_human_data.R")
```

The LLM side of the same 458 novel binomials people judged. Scores come from
`Scripts/score_llm_prefs.py`, which records, for every (model, prompt, item),

$$\texttt{preference} = \log P(\text{word1 and word2}) - \log P(\text{word2 and word1})$$

so `preference` is the model's log-odds of the alphabetical order and is directly
comparable to the logit-scale quantity the human bernoulli models estimate.

The specification mirrors `human_prefs_analysis.Rmd` with two substitutions,
which are the same ones used in LLM-Ordering-Preferences:

- the outcome is Gaussian on the log-odds scale rather than a bernoulli choice,
  because each cell yields a continuous score rather than a single click;
- `prompt_value` takes the place of `participant` as the repeated-measures
  grouping factor. A model is a model, not a sample of models, so each one is fit
  on its own and the models are compared afterwards rather than pooled.

```{r config}
LLM_DIR    <- "../Data/llm-prefs"
HUMAN_DIR  <- "../Data/human-responses"
MIN_CHECKS <- 8
ITER <- 4000; WARMUP <- 2000; CHAINS <- 4; CORES <- 4
SEED <- 964

## Fitting every model takes hours. Set this to a character vector of model names
## (or families) to work on a subset while developing.
FIT_ONLY <- NULL

## Sum coding, matching human_prefs_analysis.Rmd so the two sides are
## parameterised the same way. Set in every analysis script in this project,
## whether or not the current models contain a factor; here it starts mattering
## the moment `model` or `model_family` enters a pooled `AbsPref_c * model` fit.
##
## Both slots: the first applies to unordered factors, the second to ordered
## ones (R defaults those to contr.poly).
options(contrasts = c("contr.sum", "contr.sum"))

## brms reads cached fits from `file=` without refitting, so models estimated
## before this option was set keep their old parameterisation. Clear models/ to
## re-estimate under sum coding.
## Defined properly once the human data is loaded; defaulted here so a chunk
## option can never be evaluated before it exists.
human_ready <- FALSE

dir.create("models", showWarnings = FALSE)
set.seed(SEED)
```

# Data

```{r load}
llm    <- load_llm_data(LLM_DIR, models = FIT_ONLY)
scores <- llm$scores
items  <- llm$items
```

```{r coverage}
llm$coverage %>%
  knitr::kable(caption = "One row per scored model. `n_items` should be 458 and
                          `n_prompts` 51 everywhere; anything lower means that
                          model's run was interrupted and should be resumed.")
```

# Abstract preference

`AbsPref` is the Morgan & Levy abstract preference, computed by the same
`add_abs_pref()` the human analysis uses (`constraints.R`). Centring at 0.5 makes
the intercept the model's log-odds of the alphabetical order for an item with no
abstract preference either way, which is the bias term: a model that simply likes
whichever order it saw first, or alphabetical order as a spelling artefact, shows
up here rather than in the slope.

Each specification is fit twice: once as stated, and once with the corpus
bigram log-odds added. The bigram arm is the surface-statistics control. The
trigram "word1 and word2" is zero for every item by construction, so the
strongest available n-gram baseline is built from the component bigrams
(`Scripts/compute_bigram_logodds.py`), corpus-matched per family: Pythia against
the Pile, the hand-trained models against BabyLM, everything else against Dolma.

If an effect survives the bigram arm, it is not reducible to the corpus's
positional statistics.

```{r m-abspref, results="hide"}
## One fit per model per arm. `file =` caches each to models/, so an interrupted
## run resumes rather than refitting everything, and the two arms never collide
## because the bigram arm carries its own filename prefix.
fit_abspref <- function(model_name, with_bigram = FALSE) {
  d <- scores %>% filter(model == model_name)
  rhs <- if (with_bigram) "AbsPref_c + bigram_logodds_z" else "AbsPref_c"
  f <- as.formula(paste("preference ~", rhs,
                        "+ (AbsPref_c | prompt_value) + (1 | Item)"))
  brm(
    f, data = d, family = gaussian(),
    iter = ITER, warmup = WARMUP, chains = CHAINS, cores = CORES, seed = SEED,
    file = file.path("models", paste0(if (with_bigram) "llm_abspref_bg_"
                                      else "llm_abspref_",
                                      make.names(model_name)))
  )
}

model_names  <- levels(droplevels(scores$model))
abspref_fits    <- set_names(map(model_names, fit_abspref), model_names)
abspref_bg_fits <- set_names(map(model_names, fit_abspref, with_bigram = TRUE),
                             model_names)
```

```{r abspref-coefs}
model_meta <- scores %>%
  distinct(model, model_family, params) %>%
  mutate(model = as.character(model))

abspref_coefs <- imap_dfr(abspref_fits, function(fit, model_name) {
  as_draws_df(fit) %>%
    select(b_Intercept, b_AbsPref_c) %>%
    pivot_longer(everything(), names_to = "term", values_to = "estimate") %>%
    group_by(term) %>%
    summarise(median = median(estimate),
              q2.5   = quantile(estimate, 0.025),
              q97.5  = quantile(estimate, 0.975),
              pct_above_zero = 100 * mean(estimate > 0),
              .groups = "drop") %>%
    mutate(model = model_name)
}) %>%
  left_join(model_meta, by = "model")

abspref_coefs %>%
  filter(term == "b_AbsPref_c") %>%
  arrange(params) %>%
  select(model, model_family, params, median, q2.5, q97.5, pct_above_zero) %>%
  knitr::kable(digits = 3,
               caption = "Sensitivity to abstract preference, one row per model.")
```

## Does abstract preference survive the bigram control?

The question the second arm exists to answer. If `AbsPref_c` keeps its
coefficient once the corpus's positional statistics are in the model, it is
measuring something the n-gram baseline does not capture. If it collapses, the
apparent constraint sensitivity was surface statistics all along.

```{r abspref-bigram-compare}
bg_coefs <- imap_dfr(abspref_bg_fits, function(fit, model_name) {
  as_draws_df(fit) %>%
    select(any_of(c("b_AbsPref_c", "b_bigram_logodds_z"))) %>%
    pivot_longer(everything(), names_to = "term", values_to = "estimate") %>%
    group_by(term) %>%
    summarise(median = median(estimate),
              q2.5 = quantile(estimate, 0.025),
              q97.5 = quantile(estimate, 0.975),
              .groups = "drop") %>%
    mutate(model = model_name)
}) %>% left_join(model_meta, by = "model")

abspref_coefs %>%
  filter(term == "b_AbsPref_c") %>%
  select(model, params, abspref_alone = median) %>%
  left_join(bg_coefs %>% filter(term == "b_AbsPref_c") %>%
              select(model, abspref_with_bigram = median), by = "model") %>%
  left_join(bg_coefs %>% filter(term == "b_bigram_logodds_z") %>%
              select(model, bigram = median), by = "model") %>%
  mutate(shrinkage = 1 - abspref_with_bigram / abspref_alone) %>%
  arrange(params) %>%
  knitr::kable(digits = 3,
               caption = "AbsPref alone vs with the bigram control, and the
                          bigram coefficient itself. `shrinkage` is the
                          proportion of the AbsPref effect the control absorbs;
                          near 0 means the two are measuring different things.")
```

## Does sensitivity scale?

```{r plot-scale, fig.width=8, fig.height=5.5}
abspref_coefs %>%
  filter(term == "b_AbsPref_c") %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = params, y = median, colour = model_family)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey50") +
  geom_pointrange(aes(ymin = q2.5, ymax = q97.5)) +
  geom_line(aes(group = model_family), alpha = 0.4) +
  geom_text_repel(aes(label = model), size = 2.6, show.legend = FALSE,
                  max.overlaps = 20) +
  scale_x_log10(labels = scales::label_comma(suffix = "M")) +
  labs(x = "Parameters (log scale)",
       y = "AbsPref coefficient (log-odds)",
       colour = "Family",
       caption = "Posterior medians with 95% credible intervals.
                  Lines join models within a family.") +
  theme_bw()
```

Within a family the line is the scale trend with architecture and training data
held constant; across families the vertical spread at a given size is what
training data and recipe buy. The BabyLM models sit at the small end on a
human-sized corpus, so the gap between them and a same-size model trained on
orders of magnitude more text is the data-quantity comparison.

## Intercepts

```{r abspref-intercepts}
abspref_coefs %>%
  filter(term == "b_Intercept") %>%
  arrange(desc(abs(median))) %>%
  select(model, model_family, params, median, q2.5, q97.5) %>%
  knitr::kable(digits = 3,
               caption = "Baseline preference for the alphabetical order at
                          AbsPref = 0.5. Far from zero means a standing bias
                          independent of the constraints.")
```

# Item-level agreement with people

Aggregating to one point per binomial is the most direct human/LLM comparison,
and it needs no scale assumption on either side.

```{r human-load}
d_human <- load_human_data(HUMAN_DIR, min_checks = MIN_CHECKS)
paired  <- join_human_llm(items, d_human$trials)
```

```{r agreement-table}
paired %>%
  group_by(model, model_family, params) %>%
  summarise(
    pearson  = cor(llm_preference, human_logodds),
    spearman = cor(llm_preference, human_logodds, method = "spearman"),
    ## Do the two sides at least pick the same order?
    direction_agreement = mean((llm_p > 0.5) == (human_p > 0.5)),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  arrange(desc(spearman)) %>%
  knitr::kable(digits = 3,
               caption = "LLM preference against human preference, over the 458
                          items. Correlations are on the log-odds scale;
                          direction agreement is scale-free.")
```

```{r plot-agreement, fig.width=9, fig.height=8}
paired %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = human_p, y = llm_p)) +
  geom_abline(intercept = 0, slope = 1, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey50") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0.5, linewidth = 0.2, colour = "grey85") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0.5, linewidth = 0.2, colour = "grey85") +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.3, size = 0.7) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, colour = "steelblue", linewidth = 0.6) +
  facet_wrap(~ fct_reorder(model, params)) +
  coord_equal(xlim = c(0, 1), ylim = c(0, 1)) +
  labs(x = "Human preference for the alphabetical order",
       y = "Model preference, averaged over prompts",
       caption = "Dashed line is identity.") +
  theme_bw(base_size = 8)
```

A model can track people's *ranking* closely while sitting far off the identity
line, because nothing forces its log-odds onto the same scale as a choice
proportion. Read the correlation columns for ranking and the plot for calibration.

# Individual constraints

The same simultaneous-constraint model the human analysis fits, with `Icon`
dropped because every novel item is coded 0.

```{r m-constraints, results="hide"}
constraint_terms <- c("Form", "Percept", "Culture", "Power", "Intense",
                      "Freq", "Len", "Lapse", "BStress")

## By-prompt random slopes for every constraint, matching the specification in
## the earlier version of this work. The constraints vary within prompt (each
## prompt sees all 444 items), so the slopes are licensed; and with 51 prompts
## against 444 items they are better identified than a per-participant slope
## would be. If a fit fails to converge, CONSTRAINT_SLOPES can be set FALSE to
## fall back to random intercepts rather than silently keeping a bad fit.
CONSTRAINT_SLOPES <- TRUE

fit_constraints <- function(model_name, with_bigram = FALSE) {
  d <- scores %>% filter(model == model_name)
  terms <- if (with_bigram) c(constraint_terms, "bigram_logodds_z")
           else constraint_terms
  re <- if (CONSTRAINT_SLOPES) paste(terms, collapse = " + ") else "1"
  f <- as.formula(paste("preference ~", paste(terms, collapse = " + "),
                        "+ (", re, "| prompt_value) + (1 | Item)"))
  brm(
    f, data = d, family = gaussian(),
    iter = ITER, warmup = WARMUP, chains = CHAINS, cores = CORES, seed = SEED,
    file = file.path("models", paste0(if (with_bigram) "llm_constraints_bg_"
                                      else "llm_constraints_",
                                      make.names(model_name)))
  )
}

constraint_fits    <- set_names(map(model_names, fit_constraints), model_names)
constraint_bg_fits <- set_names(map(model_names, fit_constraints, with_bigram = TRUE),
                                model_names)
```

```{r constraint-coefs}
llm_constraint_coefs <- imap_dfr(constraint_fits, function(fit, model_name) {
  as_draws_df(fit) %>%
    select(starts_with("b_"), -b_Intercept) %>%
    pivot_longer(everything(), names_to = "term", values_to = "estimate") %>%
    mutate(term = str_remove(term, "^b_")) %>%
    group_by(term) %>%
    summarise(median = median(estimate),
              q2.5   = quantile(estimate, 0.025),
              q97.5  = quantile(estimate, 0.975),
              pct_above_zero = 100 * mean(estimate > 0),
              .groups = "drop") %>%
    mutate(model = model_name)
}) %>%
  left_join(model_meta, by = "model")
```

```{r plot-constraints, fig.width=9, fig.height=7}
llm_constraint_coefs %>%
  mutate(term = fct_reorder(term, median)) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = median, y = term, colour = model_family)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey50") +
  geom_pointrange(aes(xmin = q2.5, xmax = q97.5),
                  position = position_dodge(width = 0.6), size = 0.2) +
  labs(x = "Coefficient (log-odds of the alphabetical order)",
       y = NULL, colour = "Family",
       caption = "Posterior medians with 95% credible intervals, one estimate
                  per model per constraint.") +
  theme_bw()
```

## Against the human weights

The two sides are on different scales, so this is about sign and relative
ordering, not magnitude.

```{r human-constraints}
## Refits nothing when human_prefs_analysis.Rmd has already cached the model;
## brm(file = ) reads it back. But with only a handful of participants a
## by-participant variance has nothing to estimate, so this is skipped rather
## than fit on data that cannot support it. Everything downstream of it is
## guarded on `human_ready`.
MIN_PARTICIPANTS_FOR_FIT <- 10
trials_c <- d_human$trials
n_participants <- nlevels(droplevels(trials_c$participant))
human_ready <- n_participants >= MIN_PARTICIPANTS_FOR_FIT ||
               file.exists("models/m_constraints.rds")

if (!human_ready) {
  message("human constraint model skipped: ", n_participants,
          " participant(s), need ", MIN_PARTICIPANTS_FOR_FIT,
          ". The LLM-side results above are unaffected.")
}
```

```{r human-constraints-fit, eval = human_ready}
f_human <- as.formula(paste(
  "alpha_answer ~", paste(constraint_terms, collapse = " + "),
  "+ (1 | participant) + (1 | Item)"
))

m_constraints_human <- brm(
  f_human, data = trials_c, family = bernoulli(link = "logit"),
  iter = ITER, warmup = WARMUP, chains = CHAINS, cores = CORES, seed = SEED,
  file = "models/m_constraints"
)

human_coefs <- as_draws_df(m_constraints_human) %>%
  select(starts_with("b_"), -b_Intercept) %>%
  pivot_longer(everything(), names_to = "term", values_to = "estimate") %>%
  mutate(term = str_remove(term, "^b_")) %>%
  group_by(term) %>%
  summarise(human_median = median(estimate), .groups = "drop")
```

```{r weight-agreement, eval = human_ready}
llm_constraint_coefs %>%
  inner_join(human_coefs, by = "term") %>%
  group_by(model, model_family, params) %>%
  summarise(
    weight_pearson  = cor(median, human_median),
    weight_spearman = cor(median, human_median, method = "spearman"),
    sign_agreement  = mean(sign(median) == sign(human_median)),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  arrange(desc(weight_spearman)) %>%
  knitr::kable(digits = 3,
               caption = "How closely each model's fitted constraint weights
                          track the human ones, across the nine constraints.")
```

```{r plot-weights, fig.width=9, fig.height=8, eval = human_ready}
llm_constraint_coefs %>%
  inner_join(human_coefs, by = "term") %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = human_median, y = median)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linewidth = 0.2, colour = "grey70") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linewidth = 0.2, colour = "grey70") +
  geom_pointrange(aes(ymin = q2.5, ymax = q97.5), size = 0.2) +
  geom_text_repel(aes(label = term), size = 2.2, max.overlaps = 20) +
  facet_wrap(~ fct_reorder(model, params), scales = "free_y") +
  labs(x = "Human weight (log-odds)",
       y = "Model weight (log-odds)") +
  theme_bw(base_size = 8)
```

A model that has learned the human constraint profile puts the points on an
upward line through the origin. One that has learned a different profile puts
them somewhere else, and *which* constraints move is the interesting part:
`Freq` and `Len` are recoverable from distributional statistics alone, while
`Power`, `Culture` and `Percept` are semantic and have no direct surface cue.

# Prompt sensitivity

How much does the frame move the estimate? If a model's preference swings with
the prefix, a single-prompt result from it would not have replicated.

```{r prompt-sd}
scores %>%
  group_by(model, model_family, params, item_id) %>%
  summarise(sd_across_prompts = sd(preference), .groups = "drop") %>%
  group_by(model, model_family, params) %>%
  summarise(median_sd = median(sd_across_prompts),
            q95_sd    = quantile(sd_across_prompts, 0.95),
            .groups   = "drop") %>%
  arrange(params) %>%
  knitr::kable(digits = 3,
               caption = "Within-item spread of preference across the 51 prompts.
                          Compare with the AbsPref coefficients above: a model
                          whose prompt spread dwarfs its AbsPref effect is not
                          giving a stable preference.")
```
